headline: City Council Debates Whether Pigeons Count as Residents for Census Purposes
summary: Three-hour session produces no resolution, extensive discussion of 'what it means to belong somewhere.'
content:
What was scheduled as a routine city council meeting Tuesday evening extended well past its allotted time when Councilwoman Patricia Huang raised what she called "a question of civic philosophy": should the city's pigeon population be counted in local census figures?

"These birds have been here longer than most of us," Huang argued. "They were born here. They raise their families here. They contribute to the ecosystem. By any reasonable definition, they are residents."

The motion, which Huang acknowledged was "largely symbolic," sparked nearly three hours of debate that touched on topics including property taxes, voting rights, migration patterns, and "what it really means to belong somewhere."

Councilman David Martinez opposed the measure. "Residency implies certain responsibilities," he said. "Pigeons don't pay taxes. They don't serve on juries. They don't even acknowledge traffic laws."

"Neither do half my neighbors," responded resident Harold Finch from the public gallery, drawing scattered applause.

City demographer Dr. Lisa Park was called to provide technical context. "From a statistical standpoint, we don't count non-human animals in census data," she explained. "However, if we did, the pigeon population would represent approximately 847 additional residents in the downtown core alone."

The council ultimately tabled the motion pending further research into "precedent in other municipalities" and "whether this is something we're actually empowered to do."

Huang expressed satisfaction with the discussion. "The point was never really about the pigeons," she said after the meeting. "It was about asking ourselves who we consider part of our community. Also, a little bit about the pigeons."

The city's pigeon population could not be reached for comment.
author: Marcus Webb, City Hall Reporter
